newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-Ireland's Independent swoops on NZ publisher.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ireland's Independent swoops on NZ publisher.

text.p: Ireland's Independent Newspapers Plc launched a surprise full takeover bid for New Zealand publisher Wilson and Horton Ltd on Monday but analysts said shareholders may hold out for more.

INP said it was offering NZ$10.50 ($6.94) per share in a bid that values the New Zealand group at more than NZ$1 billion. It already holds a 22.6 percent interest, with the same amount in the hands of family trusts linked to principal Tony O'Reilly.

Wilson and Horton owns the Auckland-based New Zealand Herald, the country's biggest newspaper, and has a one-third share in a consortium that bought Radio New Zealand's commercial stations in April for NZ$89 million.
"A successful offer will further broaden and develop the international composition of the INP Group and its leading positions in newspaper publishing," INP Deputy Chairman John Meagher said.
"INP continues to be particularly attracted to the stable and progressive economic environment which New Zealand has to offer."
Analysts said the rationale for seeking 100 percent control was sound, but the timing -- within a month of New Zealand's general election -- caught the market by surprise.

They questioned whether shareholders -- who can opt for cash or take part of their entitlement in exchangeable INP preference shares -- would sell willingly at $10.50. Wilson and Horton closed on Monday at $9.70.

"Perhaps it may be seen as just a little bit opportunistic," said ANZ Securities Managing Director Tim Preston. "There may be people in the market who feel that the underlying business and the franchise...may well be worth a bit more."

John Rowley at SBC Warbug said $10.50 was a reasonable "first shot", given that the share price had been around $9.50 for some time. But he said: "My gut reaction would be (it's) probably not enough to take over such a strong franchise."
Wilson and Horton issued a notice advising shareholders not to sell for the time being, and Rowley said an expected independent appraisal of the bid would prove "intriguing".
The vehicle for the bid is Independent Press Communications Ltd (IPCL), a wholly-owned subsidiary of INP.
IPCL Chairman Michael Walls said the group saw good synergies through a full takeover. While the radio assets were "interesting", the main focus was on the newspaper side.

"The major focus, if you look at the business of our group worldwide and at the business of Wilson and Horton, is on the printed medium. We think it's got a long way to go and is far from being a spent medium," he told Reuters.
Asked about the price, he said: "We're offering New Zealanders the chance to sell out at a very fair price...If it were not for us, no one else would offer it to them."

Irish-based INP has media investments in Britain, Ireland, South Africa, France, Portugal, Mexico and Australasia. It said Wilson and Horton would account for more than 40 percent of the enlarged group's assets if it won 100 percent ownership.
